newsitem.title: USA: Environment shaping up as key issue in the West.
newsitem.headline: Environment shaping up as key issue in the West.

text.p: A billboard on the way to downtown Denver asks "Are we becoming L.A.?"

In the Rocky Mountain states, where environmental concerns carry strong political clout, this may be more than a sign of the times, symbolising public fears that the scenic terrain may be overrun by urban sprawl and may one day look like smog-choked Los Angeles. As a result, environmental issues are playing a key role in the upcoming elections.
Examples are a voter initiative on clean water in Montana and what is turning out to be a bitter battle for a Senate seat in Colorado being vacated by Republican Hank Brown.
Republicans say the Clinton administration has been waging a war on the West and argue that protection of the environment can be achieved along with economic development.
Democrats, running against Republican House Speaker Newt Gingrich as much as their own opponents, contend voters do not want to roll back environmental protections.
Polls show women voters in particular fear the Republican revolution would jeopardise national treasures.

In Colorado the Democratic candidate for the U.S. Senate, Tom Strickland, has been lambasted by his Republican opponent, Representative Wayne Allard, as a lobbyist for polluters. Strickland has defended his record on the environment, saying his law firm has represented clients responsibly, and he has accused Allard in turn of not caring enough about the environment.

Strickland has been able to capture key endorsements from environmental groups. Allard has said he wants more local control of environmental issues rather than having the bureaucracy in Washington call the shots.

"The Democratic Party in Colorado is generally seen as more environmentally oriented," said Rodney Hero, a political science professor at the University of Colorado at Boulder. "The well-being of the state is related to or tied to environmental protection. Democrats are more assertive. Republicans argue balance."
Polls show the race in Colorado is close.
But in New Mexico, the Green Party seeks to put the two major parties on the defensive.

"We're putting the duopoly's feet to the fire," said Judy Gonzales, spokeswoman for Green Party senatorial candidate Abraham Gutmann who is running against popular Republican Sen. Pete Domenici. Gutmann is registering only single-digit support in polls, however.
The Democratic candidate for senator is Art Trujillo, a former mayor of Santa Fe, New Mexico
President Clinton's recent decision to set aside 1.7 million acres in southern Utah as a national monument safe from development has stirred the pot in New Mexico.

Democratic Representative Bill Orton recently distanced himself from his party in order to save face with constituents after Clinton created the national monument, which jeopardises the creation of good paying jobs in a coal mine that had been planned in the area. Orton is seeking a fourth term in Utah's vast and sparsely populated third district that covers the area from Provo to the Arizona border.

Orton worked with Utah's Republican Gov. Mike Leavitt to win 11th-hour compromises from the administration that addressed local concerns about the new monument, such as retaining grazing and hunting rights on the land. How much that will help Orton remains to be seen.
Orton, whose personal appeal has helped him maintain popularity with voters in the heavily Republican district, faces Republican Chris Cannon in November.

In Montana, voters must decide on a water quality initiative that would require stricter water treatment standards for new or expanding mineral mines -- an important economic force in the Big Sky state. The emotionally charged issue has become a battle of the scientists, with mining companies arguing they can neither afford nor even reach the type of standard Initiative 122 would require.
